i OurBigBook.com
Put α=N​. Every positive solution satisfies
0<yx​−α=y2(x/y+α)M​<2y21​.
(1)
After reducing x/y=p/q, we still have ∣α−p/q∣<1/(2q2). Here is the continued fraction convergent criterion with its proof. If p/q is reduced and obeys this inequality, it is a strict best approximation of the second kind: for any different r/s with 0<s≤q, the assumption ∣sα−r∣≤∣qα−p∣ would give
1≤∣ps−qr∣≤s∣p−qα∣+q∣r−sα∣<2qs+q​≤1,
(2)
a contradiction. Choose consecutive continued fraction convergents pj​/qj​,pj+1​/qj+1​ with qj​≤q<qj+1​. Their determinant is ±1, their errors ej​=qj​α−pj​ alternate in sign, and every integer pair (r,s) is uniquely a(pj​,qj​)+b(pj+1​,qj+1​). For 0<s<qj+1​, either b=0, or a,b have opposite signs: positive a,b would make s≥qj+1​, negative a,b make s<0, and a=0 is impossible. Opposite signs make aej​ and bej+1​ have the same sign, so ∣sα−r∣≥∣ej​∣. If b=0, reduction gives the jth convergent itself. Thus a strict best approximation must be a convergent. The determinant and alternating-error facts follow immediately from the recurrence pj​=aj​pj−1​+pj−2​, qj​=aj​qj−1​+qj−2​ and the positive continued-fraction tail formula. Therefore the reduced ratio x/y is a convergent of N​. Without assuming gcd(x,y)=1, the unreduced pair may be a common multiple of the convergent's numerator and denominator; for example (10,2) for N=24,M=4 reduces to 5/1.

i OurBigBook.com
Take the holomorphic function f(z)=1/z on a neighborhood of the annulus. Every polynomial has integral zero around the unit circle by the Cauchy integral theorem, while ∫∣z∣=1​z−1dz=2πi. Uniform convergence on the annulus would imply convergence of these contour integrals, since their difference is bounded by 2π times the uniform error. Thus uniform polynomial approximation on the full annulus need not exist.

Kj​={z:1/2≤∣z∣≤2,1/j≤argz≤2π−1/j}.
(4)
These compact sets increase to the slit annulus, and each has connected complement: the omitted angular corridor joins the inner disk to the outside of the outer disk. The polynomial Runge theorem says that a function holomorphic near a compact set with connected complement can be approximated uniformly there by polynomials. Choose pj​ with supKj​​∣pj​−f∣<1/j. Every compact subset K of the slit annulus has positive distance from the removed positive ray, so K⊆Kj​ for all sufficiently large j. Hence pj​→f uniformly on every such compact subset.

3F (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 324 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 324
3F OurBigBook.com
Let Hk​ be the open hyperbolic half-plane beyond γk​, opposite the central region U. These three half-planes have disjoint closures in the disk, and hyperbolic reflection Jk​ exchanges Hk​ and its complementary half-plane. In particular Jk​(U∘)⊂Hk​ and Ji​(Hj​)⊂Hi​ when i=j. A reduced nonempty reflection word therefore sends an interior point of U into the half-plane corresponding to its first letter. It cannot be the identity. This ping-pong lemma argument proves that the reflection group is
W=⟨J1​,J2​,J3​∣J12​=J22​=J32​=1⟩≅C2​∗C2​∗C2​.
(6)
The usual reflection tiling makes U a fundamental domain for W: successive reflection across an offending side reduces a point to U, and the disjoint-side configuration yields locally finite tiles. Equivalently this is the disjoint-geodesic case of the reflection fundamental-domain theorem; there are no vertex relations because the sides never meet.
The orientation-preserving subgroup consists of even words. Every pair Ji​Jj​ can be expressed in A=J2​J1​ and B=J3​J2​: the other nontrivial pairs are their inverses and J3​J1​=BA, J1​J3​=A−1B−1. Thus it is exactly G. A fundamental set is U∪J2​U, with one representative chosen on each paired side; its interior is a fundamental domain. To see there are no relations between A,B, the reflection-word tree has vertices the reduced words and edges joining w to wJi​. The even subgroup acts freely on this tree; its quotient has two vertices joined by three edges. Choosing the J2​ edge as a spanning tree leaves two independent loops, represented by A and B. Reduced loops in a graph form a free group, so
G≅F2​ freely on A,B.​
(7)
The quotient is the double of the central three-sided region along its geodesic sides: an orientable pair of pants, topologically a sphere with three points removed. Its three ends are hyperbolic funnels, not cusps, because the sides are ultraparallel and the peripheral transformations have positive translation lengths. The compact convex core has three geodesic boundary circles; the complete quotient itself has no boundary.

4H (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 176 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 176
4H OurBigBook.com
A linear code of length n over Fq​ is a linear subspace C⊆Fqn​. A parity-check matrix P satisfies C=kerP. Its minimum distance of a code is the least Hamming distance between distinct codewords, equivalently the least Hamming weight of a nonzero word, because differences remain in the code.
For the usual binary bar product of binary linear codes, take equal-length binary codes with C2​⊆C1​ and define
C1​∣C2​={(u,u+v):u∈C1​, v∈C2​}.
(8)
It is linear, of length 2n and dimension dimC1​+dimC2​, since the parametrization is injective. If v=0 and the word is nonzero, its weight is 2wt(u)≥2d(C1​). If v=0, coordinatewise wt(u)+wt(u+v)≥wt(v)≥d(C2​). The words (u,u) with u of minimum nonzero weight and (0,v) with v of minimum weight achieve the two candidate bounds. Thus
d(C1​∣C2​)=min{2d(C1​),d(C2​)}.​
(9)
For a word (x,y), membership is equivalent to P1​x=0 and P2​(x+y)=0. Consequently a parity-check matrix of a bar product is
(P1​P2​​0P2​​).​
(10)
The same distance argument actually needs only equal block lengths and a common field, not nesting. Over a general field replace the second row block by (−P2​,P2​), so it tests y−x∈C2​. The displayed binary construction uses the conventional nesting.

Solution

Words: 112
5J OurBigBook.com
Assume n>p≥1, the ordinary nonsaturated Gaussian linear model. The log likelihood is, up to a constant,
ℓ(β,σ2)=−2n​logσ2−2σ2∥Y−Xβ∥2​.
(11)
The normal equations and full column rank give the least-squares estimator β​=(XTX)−1XTY. Write H=X(XTX)−1XT and Q=I−H, an orthogonal projection of rank n−p. Maximizing in σ2 yields
σ2=nYTQY​.​
(12)
Since QX=0, the residual sum of squares is εTQε. Expanding its expectation uses only Eεi​εj​=σ2δij​:
E(YTQY)=∑i,j​Qij​E(εi​εj​)=σ2trQ=(n−p)σ2.
(13)
This does not use Cochran's theorem. It proves bias −pσ2/n and gives
Eσ2=(1−p/n)σ2,σ2=n−pYTQY​,Eσ2=σ2.​
(14)
In the saturated case n=p, residuals vanish identically, the likelihood is unbounded as the positive variance tends to zero, and the unbiased residual estimator is unavailable. Thus the usual variance-estimation request requires n>p.

6A (Mathematical Biology)

Solution

Words: 136
6A OurBigBook.com
With no chemotaxis, the stationary oxygen equation is Dc​c′′=knˉ. Symmetry and the two prescribed surface values give
c(z)=c0​+2Dc​knˉ​(z2−4d2​).​
(15)
By Fick's first law, the vertical oxygen flux is jc​=−Dc​c′=−knˉz. Thus each face supplies an inward flux knˉd/2 per unit area, and the total influx is knˉd, equal to the integrated consumption across the layer. The profile is physically nonnegative only if c0​≥knˉd2/(8Dc​); otherwise the constant-consumption approximation must be modified.
For bacteria retained in the fluid, impose zero bacterial flux at the faces. The stationary bacterial equation says that jn​=−Dn​n′+μnc′ is constant, hence zero. Integrating n′/n=(μ/Dn​)c′ gives n(z)=n0​exp(μc(z)/Dn​), with n0​ fixed by the total bacterial population. Substitution into the oxygen equation proves
c′′−Dc​kn0​​exp(μc/Dn​)=0.​
(16)
Zero bacterial through-flux is the boundary assumption behind this equilibrium relation.

7D (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 251 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 251
7D OurBigBook.com
Use binary expansions ending in zeros at dyadic rationals. The doubling map shifts the expansion left:
x=0.b1​b2​b3​…⟹F(x)=0.b2​b3​b4​….
(17)
In ordinary coordinates it is 2x on [0,1/2) and 2x−1 on [1/2,1). The branches are continuous; the left limit at 1/2 is 1 while its value and right limit are 0. This is its only discontinuity in the half-open interval.
For every N≥2, the repeating binary block 0N−11 gives
xN​=2N−11​,FN(xN​)=xN​.​
(18)
Its least period is N: a shorter repeating block would make more than one digit equal to one in a length-N period. The orbit avoids the discontinuity, and its multiplier is (FN)′=2N>1, so these periodic orbits are repelling and unstable. The same multiplier argument applies to every periodic orbit, with the endpoint fixed point treated one-sidedly.
In the two-branch horseshoe formulation of Glendinning chaos, disjoint subintervals are each mapped onto the same interval by an iterate. Here J=(0,1), K0​=(0,1/2) and K1​=(1/2,1) already satisfy F(K0​)=F(K1​)=J. Their inverse branches x↦x/2 and x↦(x+1)/2 realize every binary itinerary. This is a horseshoe for a piecewise continuous map; on the circle the endpoint jump disappears. The symbolic explanation also shows dense periodic points, by repeating any prescribed finite prefix, and topological transitivity, because an iterate maps any sufficiently small dyadic cylinder onto (0,1). Finally every neighborhood contains points sharing an arbitrarily long prefix but with different subsequent digits; an appropriate iterate separates their images by a fixed amount, for instance more than 1/4. This proves sensitive dependence on initial conditions as well. The binary shift has full two-symbol chaotic dynamics.

(1−e−x)−2=∑j=0∞​(j+1)e−jx,(ex−1)−2=∑m=2∞​(m−1)e−mx.

If σ=ℜz>1, the sum of integrals of absolute values is

Solution

Words: 205
9D OurBigBook.com
The quadratic first integrals of the torque-free Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body are
2E=I1​ω12​+I2​ω22​+I3​ω32​,L2=I12​ω12​+I22​ω22​+I32​ω32​.​
(22)
Differentiation and substitution of all three Euler equations make each derivative vanish: the coefficients respectively sum to (I2​−I3​)+(I3​−I1​)+(I1​−I2​)=0 and I1​(I2​−I3​)+I2​(I3​−I1​)+I3​(I1​−I2​)=0. At either endpoint these constants are 2E=I2​Ω2, L2=I22​Ω2, proving L2=2EI2​.
Eliminating the other squared components gives, with s=ω2​/Ω,
ω12​=I1​(I3​−I1​)I2​(I3​−I2​)​Ω2(1−s2),ω32​=I3​(I3​−I1​)I2​(I2​−I1​)​Ω2(1−s2).
(23)
Hence ∣s∣≤1 and the second Euler equation gives ds/dτ=±(1−s2), where τ=Ωt(I2​−I1​)(I3​−I2​)/(I1​I3​)​ increases with t. The specified orbit goes from s=1 to s=−1, so its sign must be negative. The sign in the original PDF's reduced equation is therefore inconsistent with its endpoint conditions. The corrected heteroclinic satisfies
dτds​=s2−1,s(τ)=−tanh(τ−τ0​).​
(24)
Integrating by separation gives this family for ∣s∣<1; the integration constant is a time translation. The printed positive-sign equation instead has the increasing solutions s=tanh(τ−τ0​) and cannot meet the stated endpoints. For completeness its other real solutions are s=±1 and the branches s=coth(τ−τ0​) on intervals avoiding their pole. These latter branches are excluded by the conserved-energy constraint ∣s∣≤1. The scalar heteroclinic is unique up to translation. For the full angular-velocity vector there are two sign-related branches: simultaneously reversing ω1​ and ω3​ preserves all three Euler equations and both endpoints. Full-vector uniqueness therefore also requires choosing one of those branches.

10D (Cosmology)

Solution

Words: 142
10D OurBigBook.com
For a comoving fluid volume, V∝a3 and E=ρc2V. The first-law relation dE=−PdV gives c2(Vdρ+ρdV)=−PdV. Since V˙/V=3a˙/a, the cosmological perfect-fluid continuity equation is
ρ˙​=−3aa˙​(ρ+c2P​).​
(25)
For the Newtonian energy argument, assume negligible pressure, spherical homogeneity, Newtonian gravity and constant enclosed mass. A test particle at physical radius r=aχ has constant specific energy
ϵ=21​r˙2−rGM​,M=34π​ρr3.
(26)
Divide by a2χ2/2 and set k=−2ϵ/(c2χ2) to obtain the Friedmann equation
(aa˙​)2=38πGρ​−a2kc2​.​
(27)
Homogeneity makes k independent of the chosen comoving shell. In the relativistic interpretation it specifies the spatial-curvature sign: positive, zero or negative k gives closed spherical, flat or open hyperbolic spatial geometry, with a conventional rescaling allowing k=1,0,−1. Newtonian mechanics itself derives the energy constant, not the spatial metric. When pressure is appreciable, the general relativistic equations still have the displayed Friedmann form, but the constant-mass Newtonian test-particle derivation cannot be applied without that qualification.

11G (Number Theory)

Words: 309 Articles: 5
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 163
11G OurBigBook.com
The Miller-Rabin primality test first handles 2,3 as prime and n<2 or even n>2 as composite. For odd n>3, write n−1=2sd with d odd and choose a base 2≤a≤n−2. A nontrivial gcd(a,n) proves compositeness. Otherwise compute x=admodn: the round passes if x=1 or x=−1. If neither holds, square successively, at most s−1 times, and pass if a value −1 occurs; otherwise declare composite. An occurrence of 1 before −1 exhibits a nontrivial square root of one and is also a failure. For prime n, Fermat's theorem and the fact that a field has only the square roots ±1 force a pass. The standard strong-liar bound says that an odd composite passes for at most one quarter of the bases; independent random rounds therefore have error probability at most 4−r after r rounds. Passing is a probable-prime verdict, not a proof of primality. A Fermat pseudoprime is composite and passes an−1≡1(modn); a strong pseudoprime is composite and passes the stronger round above.

N=34p−1​=(2p−1)32p+1​

ii OurBigBook.com
By the definition of Fermat pseudoprime, M is composite as well as odd, and M∣2M−1−1. Put L=2M−1. A proper factorization M=ab makes 2a−1 a proper divisor of L, so L is composite. Now
L−1=2d,d=2M−1−1 odd,M∣d.
(30)
Since 2M≡1(modL), 2d≡1(modL). This is the first passing condition of the Miller-Rabin primality test, with s=1. Thus 2M−1 is a base-two strong pseudoprime. If “pseudoprime” were used to include primes, the compositeness conclusion would fail, for instance M=3 gives L=7; the standard composite definition matters.

i OurBigBook.com
For a continuous loop in C∖{0}, choose a continuous argument lift θ:[0,1]→R with γ(t)/∣γ(t)∣=eiθ(t). Such a lift is constructed by subdividing the interval into pieces whose images lie in an argument chart and matching the arguments at their endpoints. The winding number of a continuous closed path is
w(γ;0)=2πθ(1)−θ(0)​∈Z.​
(31)
Changing the initial lift adds one constant multiple of 2π and does not change this integer.

ii OurBigBook.com
A loop homotopy is a continuous H:[0,1]2→C∖{0} with H(0,t)=γ0​(t), H(1,t)=γ1​(t) and H(s,0)=H(s,1) for every s. Compactness gives a positive lower bound r for ∣H∣ and uniform continuity. Partition the s interval finely enough that neighboring loops η,δ satisfy ∣η(t)−δ(t)∣<r. Their quotient lies in ∣z−1∣<1, and has a single-valued continuous argument with equal endpoint values. Its winding number is zero. Arguments of a product add, so w(η)=w(δ)+w(η/δ)=w(δ). Applying this at every step proves
w(γ0​;0)=w(γ1​;0).​
(32)
This proves homotopy invariance of winding number directly, including continuous curves without differentiability.

Here the target C of g is the unit circle. The boundary loop g(e2πit) extends through the disk, so the radial homotopy g(se2πit) contracts it to a constant loop. Thus its winding number is zero. On the boundary put h(z)=g(z)/zn, also circle-valued. Adding argument lifts gives w(h)=0−n=−n. If zn+g(z) never vanished, h would avoid −1, which is the only negative real point of the unit circle. Part (iii) would give w(h)=0, contradicting n=0. Therefore there is a boundary point with zn+g(z)=0. The circle-valued hypothesis is essential; it is not a claim about arbitrary complex-valued g.

13A OurBigBook.com
Introduce dimensionless quantities S=S/S0​, I=I/S0​, x=xrS0​/D​ and t=rS0​t. Substitution and cancellation of rS02​ give the stated spatial SIR model with
λ=rS0​a​.​
(33)
Drop tildes. A travelling wave with z=x−ct obeys
cS′=IS,I′′+cI′+(S−λ)I=0.​
(34)
At the leading edge S=1,I=0, the infective equation linearizes to I′′+cI′+(1−λ)I=0. For an invading epidemic the susceptible level must exceed the removal threshold, λ<1. A nonoscillatory decaying tail has exponents
r±​=2−c±c2−4(1−λ)​​.
(35)
If the discriminant is negative, a nonzero real tail oscillates in sign, violating nonnegative infective density. Thus for a right-moving wave
c≥21−λ​,λ<1.​
(36)
This is a necessary admissibility condition from the leading-edge calculation, not by itself a global existence proof.
To derive the final size relation for an epidemic, use I=cS′/S and integrate the infective ODE across the wave. The tails have I,I′→0, giving
c(1−σ)=λ∫−∞∞​I(z)dz,∫Idz=clog(1/σ).
(37)
Therefore
σ−λlogσ=1.​
(38)
For a nontrivial epidemic 0<σ<1. The function s−λlogs is strictly convex, minimized at s=λ. For 0<λ<1 it has the trivial root 1 and one further root 0<σ<λ. For λ≥1, it exceeds one for every s<1, so only the no-epidemic root remains; this also proves the necessity of λ<1. On the nontrivial branch,

Take a uniformly random ordering of the vertices and select each vertex that precedes every neighbor. The selected set is independent: if two adjacent vertices were both selected, each would have to precede the other. Among the d(v)+1 vertices consisting of v and its neighbors, each is equally likely to come first, so the selection probability is 1/(d(v)+1). Linearity of expectation gives expected size ∑v​1/(d(v)+1). At least one ordering attains at least this average; its integer size is therefore at least the ceiling. This proves the Caro-Wei bound

Let L=F(μn​). Its Galois group embeds into (Z/nZ)×, by sending an automorphism to the exponent in its action on ζn​. It is therefore finite abelian, of order dividing φ(n). The finite case of the Fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups supplies a subgroup chain whose successive quotients are cyclic of prime order ℓ. Every such ℓ<n, since ℓ≤φ(n)<n for n>1 (and for n=2 the possible prime is 2, whose roots of unity already lie in every characteristic-zero field). Thus every intermediate base contains μℓ​, because F contains all roots of unity of orders smaller than n.
Each cyclic degree-ℓ step E′/E is a Kummer extension. Here is the relevant criterion explicitly. For a generator σ and a primitive ℓth root ζ∈E, the operator ∑j=0ℓ−1​ζ−jσj is not identically zero, by linear independence of distinct field automorphisms. Choose its nonzero value a; then σ(a)=ζa, so aℓ∈E and a∈/E. Since the degree is prime, E′=E(a) is obtained by adjoining an ℓth radical. Applying this to the subgroup chain proves F(μn​)/F is a succession of Kummer extensions.
Finally use strong induction on n, for arbitrary characteristic-zero base fields. Successively adjoining the roots ζ1​,…,ζn−1​ is contained in a Kummer tower by the induction hypothesis, applied over each current base. The just-proved assertion then adjoins ζn​ by further Kummer steps. Hence any cyclotomic extension is contained in a Kummer tower. In the given cyclotomic-and-Kummer tower for a soluble extension, replace every cyclotomic step by such a tower; enlarge subsequent steps by compositum with the new intermediate fields. Base change preserves radical adjunction and the requisite roots of unity, possibly making a step trivial. Thus every finite soluble extension is contained in a succession of Kummer extensions.

A meromorphic function on the Riemann sphere is rational: it has finitely many poles; subtract their principal parts, including a polynomial for a possible pole at infinity, and the remaining entire function is bounded at infinity, hence constant by Liouville theorem. A rational map of degree d has d preimages of a regular value, counted with multiplicity. An analytic isomorphism is bijective, so d=1, giving precisely
z⟼cz+daz+b​,ad−bc=0.​
(63)
Conversely these Möbius transformations have a Möbius inverse and extend holomorphically at their pole and infinity, so are analytic isomorphisms.
For a nonconstant analytic map f:X→Y between compact connected Riemann surfaces, the Riemann-Hurwitz formula is
2gX​−2=d(2gY​−2)+p∈X∑​(ep​−1).​
(64)
Here gX​,gY​ are genera, d is the degree (the sum of local multiplicities over any fiber), and ep​ is the local degree in coordinates where the map has the form z↦zep​. Only finitely many terms are nonzero; these are the ramification points.
For a degree-two sphere map the formula gives total ramification two. Each local degree is at most two, so there are exactly two distinct ramification points, each of local degree two. Their branch values are distinct, because one fiber cannot have multiplicity four. Choose T sending 0,∞ to the two ramification points, and S sending their values to 0,∞. Then SfT has its only zero at zero, of order two, and its only pole at infinity, of order two; it is cz2 with c=0. Rescale S by 1/c. Therefore SfT(z)=z2, as required.

Assume the first-fork choices are independent Bernoulli routings, as in Poisson thinning. Put r=2λ/3. Cars assigned to A form a Poisson process of rate λ/3, also an ordinary renewal process with independent exponential holding times of rate λ/3. The stream to the second fork is an independent Poisson process of rate r.
B receives its odd-numbered arrivals. Its initial delay is exponential of rate r, followed by independent Erlang distributions of shape two and rate r between successive B arrivals. Thus B is a delayed renewal process, not Poisson. C receives the even-numbered arrivals: its first and all subsequent holding times are independent Erlang(2,r), so C is an ordinary renewal process, not Poisson. Their holding-time density and survivor are r2te−rt and e−rt(1+rt). Both have asymptotic rate r/2=λ/3; equality of these mean rates with A does not make the processes Poisson.

A control policy specifies each control as a nonanticipating measurable function of the observed history, possibly with additional randomization. It may depend on time and the entire past; a stationary Markov policy uses only the current state. We use the standard admissibility assumptions allowing measurable choices and concatenation of continuation policies.
The dynamic programming operator is monotone: f≤g implies Lf≤Lg. Nonnegative costs give F1​≥F0​=0, so induction gives Ft+1​≥Ft​. Thus Ft​ increases pointwise to an extended nonnegative limit F∞​. Backward induction identifies Ft​ with the infimum of expected costs for the first t periods: condition on the first control and next state, then optimize the continuation. Every infinite-horizon policy has at least that finite-horizon cost, so
F∞​≤F.​
(81)
For the Bellman equation, any infinite-horizon policy, conditional on its first action and next state, has continuation cost at least F(X1​). Its total cost is therefore at least LF(x); infimizing gives F≥LF. For the reverse inequality at a state with finite LF(x), choose a first action within ε/2 of its infimum and concatenate continuation policies whose costs are within ε/(2β) of F(y) at each next state y. This produces a policy of cost at most LF(x)+ε. Such continuations are needed only at states of finite value, which have probability one under an action with finite continuation expectation. Let ε↓0. If LF(x)=∞, the first inequality already gives F(x)=∞. Therefore
F=LF.​
(82)
Let Φ=LΦ≥0, and use the permitted selector u∗​. Under the stationary policy u∗​(Xt​), repeated conditional expectation gives
Φ(x)=E[∑t=0T−1​βtc(Xt​,u∗​(Xt​))+βTΦ(XT​)].
(83)
If Φ(x) is infinite the desired comparison is immediate; otherwise these nonnegative quantities have finite expectations and the displayed recursion is legitimate. Drop the terminal term and apply monotone convergence theorem as T→∞. The policy's infinite-horizon cost is at most Φ(x), so
F(x)≤Ju∗​(x)≤Φ(x).​
(84)
Thus the value is the least nonnegative Bellman fixed point. The argument works also for β=1 because costs and the dropped terminal term are nonnegative; it makes no unwarranted contraction or finite-value assumption.

The localized site orbitals are translates, ϕn​(x)=ϕ0​(x−na) and χn​(x)=χ0​(x−na). In the tight-binding model, neglect intersite overlap and use
ψ(x,t)=∑n​(bn​(t)ϕn​(x)+cn​(t)χn​(x)).

Projecting the Schrödinger equation onto each localized orbital gives its onsite energy times its own coefficient, plus the four stated neighbor matrix elements. Thus
iℏb˙n​iℏc˙n​​=E0​bn​−A(bn−1​+bn+1​+cn−1​+cn+1​),=E1​cn​−A(cn−1​+cn+1​+bn−1​+bn+1​).​​
(108)
For the Bloch amplitudes, set z=coska. The coefficient eigenproblem is
(E0​−2Az−2Az​−2AzE1​−2Az​)(CB​)=E(CB​),
(109)
so the two energy bands are
E±​(k)=2E0​+E1​​−2Acoska±21​(E1​−E0​)2+16A2cos2ka​.​
(110)
A first Brillouin zone is −π/a≤k<π/a; wavevectors differing by 2π/a are equivalent. Put Σ=E0​+E1​, D=(E1​−E0​)2+16A2​. Each band is nonincreasing as a function of z∈[−1,1], because dE±​/dz=−2A±8A2z/(E1​−E0​)2+16A2z2​≤0. Hence
E±,min​=Σ/2−2A±D/2,E±,max​=Σ/2+2A±D/2,ΔE=E+,min​−E−,max​=D−4A.​
(111)
The extrema occur at k=0 and at the zone edge; they may be nonunique when E0​=E1​, in which case the gap vanishes. In the trial wavefunction, replacing x by x+a and reindexing n produces exactly the factor eika, verifying Bloch theorem directly.
An electrical conductor has available nearby unoccupied states in a partially filled band or overlapping bands. A band insulator has filled lower bands separated from empty higher bands by a large gap. A semiconductor has the same filled-band structure with a smaller gap, so thermal excitation or doping supplies mobile electrons and holes. Band filling and carrier availability, not just the existence of two bands, determine which description applies.

The discrete comparison principle bounds the inverse image of the residual's positive part by Ch2, while the negative first residual gives e1​≤−ch​+Ch2. Hence ∣e1​∣≥c′h​ for small h. Since ∑j=1M​sin2(πjh)=1/(2h), the full Euclidean error is bounded below by a positive constant. It cannot be O(h). Thus the boxed estimate holds for the intended smooth solution class; a regularity condition is genuinely necessary.
